items.title: Symbolon
items.text:
Trustable contracts between agents. A contract is a precise, content-addressed promise. Evidence that someone kept it can be checked by anyone.

Agents increasingly call tools, run code they generated, and rebuild software on someone's behalf. Each of those is an implicit promise that something behaves a certain way. Symbolon writes the promise down in a form a machine can check, and records signed evidence that a specific implementation kept it.

Software capabilities are the first vertical. A contract specifies a capability, and any implementation, hand-written or AI-generated, in any language, is checked against it.

  • Get started

    Install the CLI, validate a seed contract, and watch a plausible implementation fail it.

items.title: The idea in one example
items.text:
$ symbolon test contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 examples/impls/date-parse-strptime
...
✗ test_iso_requires_two_digit_month_and_day
    AssertionError
    Failing test case: test_iso_requires_two_digit_month_and_day(
        impl=impl,
        d=datetime.date(2000, 1, 1),  # or any other generated value
    )

FAIL  2 of 21 checks failed

$ symbolon test contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 examples/impls/date-parse-strict
PASS  21 checks

The first implementation looks right and passes the obvious examples, but it accepts 2000-1-1 as an ISO date. The contract's properties catch it. The second, independently written implementation passes the same contract. Neither implementation matters on its own: the contract, and the evidence that something passed it, are the asset.

items.title: What is in the repository
items.text: Contract format A directory with a manifest, a pydantic schema, examples and hypothesis properties. Identified by a SHA-256 digest of its contents. Validation symbolon validate checks structure, schema drift, examples, and that the spec is not vacuous. Testing symbolon test runs a contract's spec against an implementation in Python or any language that speaks a JSON line protocol. Attestations symbolon attest runs the spec in a sandbox and writes a signed in-toto attestation; symbolon verify --rerun reproduces it. Spec packs Product-level contracts: a brief, assumptions, obligations, and component contracts. symbolon pack validate checks them. Seeds and a pilot Three seed contracts and the lightkone pilot, a spec pack extracted from a real product and rebuilt by an AI from the pack alone.

items.title: Implementations and attestations
items.text: MVP step 2. An attestation is signed evidence that one implementation passed (or failed) one contract's spec, in a recorded sandbox and environment, on a given runner.

items.title: Implementation format
items.text:
An implementation is a directory:

my-impl/
  symbolon-impl.toml   manifest (required)
  impl.py              entrypoint file (name set in the manifest)
  requirements.lock    pinned dependencies (optional)
  ...                  any other source files

[implementation]
contract = "sha256:..."     # digest of the contract this implementation targets
entrypoint = "impl.py"      # relative .py path inside the directory
language = "python"
license = "MIT"
authors = ["..."]

[generator]                 # optional, for generated implementations
model = "..."
family = "..."              # optional: model family, for the ensemble in `symbolon diff`
language = "go"             # optional: source language, when language = "command"
prompt_digest = "sha256:..."

symbolon impl-init <dir> --contract <contract-dir> writes this manifest, pinned to the contract's current digest.

items.title: Implementations in other languages
items.text:
Set language = "command" and give the program to run:

[implementation]
contract = "sha256:..."
language = "command"
command = ["node", "impl.mjs"]   # the first element may be a file inside the directory
license = "MIT"
authors = ["..."]

The program is started once per run and speaks a line protocol: one JSON value per line.

  • Request (stdin): the input object, exactly as schema/input.json describes it.
  • Reply (stdout): {"output": <output object>}, or {"error": {"type": "ValueError", "message": "..."}}.

type names the error class that the contract's examples expect. ValueError is the convention for invalid input. Anything written to stderr is kept for diagnostics. If the process exits, the failure is reported with the tail of its stderr, and the process is restarted for the next call. The container image includes Node.js (pinned through PyPI's nodejs-wheel-binaries), so JavaScript and TypeScript implementations run there unchanged. Any other runtime needs a statically linked binary for now.

  • Identity. The implementation digest is the same framing as the contract digest (see CONTRACT_FORMAT.md), with the header symbolon-implementation-v1. It covers the source, the manifest, and the lockfile. So the same code with different dependency pins is a different implementation.
  • Dependencies. Every line of requirements.lock must be pinned with ==, and --hash lines are allowed. Packages are installed with --no-deps, so the lockfile must list the full dependency set. Installation is the only step that has network access.
  • Contract binding. attest refuses to run if the manifest's contract digest is not the digest of the contract it is given.

items.title: Running an attestation
items.text:
symbolon keygen                                        # once per runner
symbolon attest <contract-dir> <impl-dir> -o att.json  # exit code 0 = PASSED

attest copies the contract and implementation into a fresh directory, computes both digests from those copies, and runs the spec inside a sandbox. That way the digests describe exactly what ran.

items.title: Sandboxes
items.text:
container (default when Docker is reachable) process (fallback) Network none, unless the contract declares hosts none, via a separate network namespace (unshare -rn) Filesystem read-only root and inputs; 64 MB /tmp not isolated User 65534, all capabilities dropped, no-new-privileges separate user namespace Limits 1 GB memory, 1 CPU, 256 processes, contract timeout 1 GB address space, CPU time = contract timeout Image python:3.13-slim pinned by digest, plus pinned pydantic, hypothesis and Node.js the host Python and Node.js

Choose one with --sandbox container|process. Each attestation records which sandbox ran it and how it isolated the run. When a contract declares network hosts, the sandbox allows network access and the attestation's evidence strength is observed instead of reproducible.

Behind a TLS-intercepting proxy, set SYMBOLON_PIP_CERT to a CA bundle. It is used only to build the runner image and to install lockfile dependencies, and it does not change the recorded environment.

items.title: Attestation format
items.text:
An attestation is an in-toto Statement v1 using the Test Result predicate, wrapped in a DSSE envelope signed with the runner's Ed25519 key.

{
  "_type": "https://in-toto.io/Statement/v1",
  "subject": [{"name": "implementation-of:core/date-parse@1", "digest": {"sha256": "<implementation digest>"}}],
  "predicateType": "https://in-toto.io/attestation/test-result/v0.1",
  "predicate": {
    "result": "PASSED",
    "configuration": [
      {"name": "contract:core/date-parse@1", "digest": {"sha256": "<contract digest>"}},
      {"name": "environment", "digest": {"sha256": "<environment digest>"}}
    ],
    "passedTests": ["example:line 1", "property:test_round_trips_every_date"],
    "warnedTests": [],
    "failedTests": [],
    "symbolon": {
      "version": "0.1.0",
      "evidence": "reproducible",
      "spec": {"seed": 0, "max_examples": 300},
      "failures": {"<test name>": "<failure detail, including the failing case>"},
      "resources": {"wall_seconds": 2.3, "cpu_seconds": 2.29, "peak_rss_kb": 49152},
      "sandbox": {"network": "none", "filesystem": "...", "user": "...", "environment": {"sandbox": "container", "...": "..."}},
      "implementation": {"implementation": {"contract": "sha256:...", "entrypoint": "impl.py", "...": "..."}},
      "runner": {"keyid": "ed25519:<sha256 of the raw public key>", "publicKey": "<base64 raw Ed25519 key>"},
      "startedOn": "2026-10-21T12:30:00Z",
      "finishedOn": "2026-10-21T12:30:03Z"
    }
  }
}
  • Test names are example:<line and note> and property:<function name>.
  • The symbolon object extends the Test Result predicate. Tools that only know the standard predicate can ignore it.
  • The environment digest covers the inputs that decide behavior: sandbox kind, base image, Python version, OS, architecture, and package versions. It excludes machine-specific ids such as the local image id, so two runners that build the same environment get the same digest.

items.title: Verifying
items.text:
symbolon verify att.json                                  # signature and contents
symbolon verify att.json --trust runner.pub               # signer is in your trust set
symbolon verify att.json --contract C --impl I            # digests match your local copies
symbolon verify att.json --contract C --impl I --rerun    # run it again here and compare

--rerun runs the attestation again in your own sandbox and compares the result of every check. "Reproduced" means every example and property has the same outcome. That is the property a third party relies on: they don't have to trust the original runner, they can check.

The runner's public key is embedded in the attestation so the signature can always be checked. Trust is a separate question: a valid signature from a key you don't trust proves only that someone ran the tests. Pass the keys you accept with --trust.

items.title: Symbolon contract format, v1
items.text: This is the format for capability contracts, the first contract kind. A contract is a directory. Its identity is the digest of that directory's contents, and nothing else.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
contracts/<namespace>/<name>/versions/<version>/
  symbolon.toml        manifest (required)
  schema.py            pydantic Input and Output models (required)
  schema/input.json    JSON Schema generated from schema.py (required)
  schema/output.json   JSON Schema generated from schema.py (required)
  examples.jsonl       example cases (required)
  fixtures/*.json      sample data the examples share (optional)
  properties.py        property-based tests (required)
  reference/impl.py    reference implementation, used only as an oracle (optional)
  mutants/*.py         plausible wrong implementations the spec must reject (optional)

Each version of a contract sits in its own folder under versions/, so contracts/core/csv-to-records/versions/1/ and versions/2/ sit side by side. The folder name is the manifest's version. Any other files in the directory, such as a README, are part of the contract and part of its digest.

items.title: Manifest: symbolon.toml
items.text:
[contract]
id = "core/date-parse"          # namespace/name, lowercase letters, digits, hyphens
version = 1                     # integer >= 1; any schema or spec change is a new version
title = "Parse a calendar date"
description = "..."             # the prose half of the spec
regenerability = "disposable"   # "disposable" or "pinned"; "sovereign" is reserved
license = "Apache-2.0"
authors = ["..."]
forked_from = "sha256:..."      # optional: digest of the parent contract

[entrypoint]
function = "run"                # name of the function implementations must define

[requires]                      # what an implementation needs from the world
network = []                    # allowed hosts; empty means no network
credentials = []                # names only, never values
state = []
permissions = []

[spec]
seed = 0                        # hypothesis seed, for reproducible runs
max_examples = 200              # hypothesis examples per property
float_rel_tol = 1e-9            # tolerance when comparing numbers in examples
timeout_seconds = 120           # per validate or test run

[runtime]
python = ">=3.11"

Unknown keys are errors, so a typo cannot silently change a contract's meaning.

items.title: Interface: schema.py and schema/*.json
items.text: schema.py must define Input and Output as pydantic models. The JSON Schema files are generated from them with symbolon schema <dir>, and validate fails if they drift apart. The JSON Schema is the language-neutral interface. Pydantic is the authoring convenience.

items.title: Implementations
items.text:
An implementation is a Python file that defines the entrypoint function. It receives the input as plain JSON values (a dict matching schema/input.json) and returns plain JSON values matching schema/output.json. It reports invalid input by raising an exception, normally ValueError. Because implementations exchange only JSON values, any tool or model can produce one without importing Symbolon.

symbolon test accepts a single file. symbolon attest needs an implementation directory with a manifest and optional lockfile; see ATTESTATION.md.

items.title: Examples: examples.jsonl
items.text:
One JSON object per line:

{"input": {...}, "output": {...}}
{"input": {...}, "raises": "ValueError", "note": "why this must fail"}
  • Each line has input and exactly one of output or raises. note is optional.
  • raises matches the exception's class or any of its base classes, by name.
  • Numbers in outputs are compared with float_rel_tol; everything else must match exactly.
  • There must be at least two examples with different outputs.

items.title: Fixtures: fixtures/
items.text:
When many examples need the same sample data, such as a library of papers, put it in fixtures/<name>.json once. Anywhere in an example, an object whose only key is $fixture is replaced by that file's contents before the example runs:

{"input": {"papers": {"$fixture": "library.json"}, "query": "tag:ml"}, "output": {"ids": ["a", "b"]}}
  • The name must be a relative path to a .json file inside fixtures/.
  • Each example gets its own copy, so an implementation that changes its input cannot affect the next example.
  • {"$text": "name"} inserts a fixture file's text instead of parsing it, for contracts whose input is a file's raw text (any extension; CRLF becomes LF, as in the digest):
{"input": {"text": {"$text": "paperpile-import.json"}}, "output": {"written": true}}
  • Fixtures are part of the contract directory, so they are part of its digest. Everyone tests against exactly the same data.
  • Properties can read fixtures too: Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "library.json".
  • Fixtures are synthetic. Never put real customer data or credentials in a contract.

items.title: Properties: properties.py
items.text: Every function named test_* is a property. Its first parameter must be impl. impl takes an Input (or a dict) and returns a validated Output, so an implementation that returns the wrong shape fails every property. Use hypothesis @given freely. Do not use @settings, because seed and budget come from the manifest so runs are reproducible.

items.title: Mutants: mutants/*.py
items.text:
A mutant is a plausible wrong implementation: the bug a careless builder, or an AI fitting the examples, would most likely write. Each file defines the entrypoint function and starts with a docstring naming the concern it models.

"""every fourth year is a leap year, centuries included"""

import datetime as dt
...

validate runs the whole spec (examples and properties) against every mutant and fails if any mutant passes. A survivor means one of two things:

  • The spec has a gap. Add an example or property that rejects the mutant.
  • The difference is acceptable. The mutant is equivalent under the contract, or the behaviour is deliberately left open. Say so in the mutant: SURVIVES = "Equivalent: float drift stays within float_rel_tol". When a pack leaves the behaviour open, name the open obligation.

validate also fails if a mutant is marked SURVIVES but is killed, if it has no docstring, or if it is the same program as the reference or another mutant once comments and docstrings are removed. Its report line reads like mutants: spec rejects every mutant 5/6 killed, 1 documented survivor, which is the contract's kill rate. symbolon mutants shows which checks kill which mutant, and which checks kill none.

Mutants are part of the contract and its digest, so anyone can reproduce the kill rate. They are kept out of the copy given to builders by symbolon canary plant. An LLM can draft mutants from the reference and a list of concerns; keep the ones that load, differ from the reference, and model a mistake someone would make.

items.title: What symbolon validate checks
items.text:
1. The required files are present.
  2. symbolon.toml parses and matches the manifest schema.
  3. schema.py defines Input and Output.
  4. schema/*.json matches what schema.py generates.
  5. examples.jsonl is well-formed, and every example matches the schema.
  6. properties.py defines at least one property, and each property takes impl.
  7. The spec (examples and properties) passes against reference/impl.py, if present.
  8. Vacuity: the properties alone fail against an implementation that always raises, and against one that always returns the first example's output. A spec that cannot tell those apart from a real implementation is not a spec.
  9. Mutants: if mutants/ exists, every mutant fails the spec or explains with SURVIVES why it may pass (see above).
  10. If all checks pass, it prints the digest.

Steps 3 to 9 execute contract code. They run in a separate Python process (python -I -m symbolon.worker). symbolon attest runs that same worker inside a sandbox (see ATTESTATION.md).

items.title: Digest
items.text:
sha256( "symbolon-contract-v1
"
        + for each file, sorted by POSIX relative path:
            path + "
" + byte_length + "
" + content + "
" )
  • content has CRLF replaced with LF.
  • Skipped: any path component starting with ., __pycache__ directories, and .pyc or .pyo files.
  • Symlinks are an error.
  • Timestamps and permissions are not included, so the same contract has the same digest on every machine.

The digest is written as sha256:<hex>. namespace/name@version is a human-readable alias for it.

items.title: Symbolon spec pack format, v1
items.text:
A spec pack is a product contract packaged for building: what the product is for, what may be assumed about the world, and the decisions a builder must keep, each tied to the checks that pin it down. Its components are ordinary capability contracts (CONTRACT_FORMAT.md).

A pack is meant to be minimal. AI builders fill gaps well, so a pack does not spell out what any good builder would do anyway. It holds the points where good builders would choose differently and the publisher would reject one choice, the facts about the world no builder can infer, and a check for each. See design v0.5, section 4.

items.title: Layout
items.text:
packs/<namespace>/<product>/versions/<version>/
  symbolon-pack.toml    manifest: pack id, version, license, component digests (required)
  BRIEF.md              purpose, non-goals, priorities, who resolves gaps (required)
  obligations.toml      the decisions a build must keep (required)
  assumptions/*.toml    what must hold about the world, one file each
  components/<name>/versions/<version>/   capability contracts
  AGENTS.md             short guide for coding agents

items.title: BRIEF.md
items.text:
Prose for people and agents. It must have these headings (any level, any case):

  • Non-goals: what the product deliberately does not do.
  • Priorities: the order in which goals win when they conflict.
  • Who resolves gaps: who answers questions the pack does not settle.

items.title: assumptions/<name>.toml
items.text:
id = "K-single-writer"                 # K-<lowercase-name>
statement = "At most one client writes a given library at a time."
basis = "Sync is manual and libraries are personal."
monitor = "none"                       # how a deployment can watch it, or "none"

Assumptions tell builders what they need not handle, and they scope the evidence: a build that passes the pack is correct under these assumptions.

items.title: obligations.toml
items.text:
[[obligation]]
id = "search.year-last-wins"           # dot-separated lowercase words
statement = "Only the last year: term in a query applies, whatever its form."
status = "decided"                     # decided | default | open
kind = "behaviour"                     # behaviour | constraint | security | audit (default behaviour)
source = "replication"                 # extract | oracle | replication | counterexample | publisher
reason = "..."                         # required when kind = "constraint"
exactness = "exact"                    # exact | statistical (default exact)
assumes = ["K-..."]                    # optional
checks = ["search-query#test_only_the_last_year_filter_counts", "search-query#example:40"]
Status Meaning Checks decided Required At least one default Chosen by the publisher; a fork may change it if it says so At least one open Deliberately undecided; builds may differ None, since a check would decide it

A check is <component>#example:<line> (a 1-based line of that component's examples.jsonl) or <component>#<test function> (a property in its properties.py). Obligation ids are the single id scheme for tracing checks to requirements; a standalone contract can adopt the same [[obligation]] table later.

source records where the obligation's current binding came from. The share that came from replication (builders disagreed) rather than extract is a measure of how much a pack needed to say beyond the obvious, so an obligation that extraction left open and replication then decided counts as replication.

items.title: Exact and statistical obligations
items.text:
exactness says how an obligation constrains outputs, independently of its status:

Exactness Meaning Extra fields exact Every output must satisfy it; one violating output fails it None statistical The output distribution must satisfy it, for software that is random by design, such as a summarizer that calls a model samples (runs per check), alpha (accepted false-alarm rate), tolerance (its share of the disagreement budget)

An open obligation is the free case: it constrains nothing, so it takes no exactness. The terms follow the kit paper (The Probabilistic Minimal Reproduction Kit, section 5.4). The runner does not yet repeat statistical checks; until it does, the fields record what a check must do.

items.title: What symbolon pack validate checks
items.text:
1. symbolon-pack.toml, BRIEF.md and obligations.toml exist.
  2. Every component listed in the manifest is present with the same digest, and none is unlisted.
  3. BRIEF.md has the three required sections.
  4. Every assumption file is well-formed, with a unique id.
  5. Every obligation is well-formed, with a unique id.
  6. Every decided or default obligation has checks, every open one has none, every constraint has a reason, every check exists, and every assumption it names exists.
  7. A statistical obligation is not open and gives samples, alpha and tolerance; an exact one gives none of them.

It then reports obligations by status, source and exactness, assumptions and how many are monitored, and how many of the components' checks trace to an obligation. It does not run contract code; use symbolon validate on each component for that.

items.title: Pack registry
items.text: The registry is a static website. A folder of packs (packs/<owner>/<name>/versions/<n>/) is turned into plain files that any web host can serve, and symbolon pull reads them. There is no server. Only the latest version of each pack is published; older versions stay in the registry's folders and git history so that attestations naming them can still be re-checked.

items.title: Making a pack
items.text:
symbolon pack init acme/invoice-desk          # creates spec/ next to your code
symbolon pack validate spec

pack init writes a manifest, a BRIEF.md with the three required headings, an obligations.toml with one open placeholder, a placeholder assumption, an empty components/ and an AGENTS.md. It passes pack validate as it stands. The generated AGENTS.md also tells the publisher's own coding agent to keep the pack current while it builds: record each choice the user makes that a builder could not have guessed as an obligation with a check, and each fact about the world as an assumption.

Holdout tests must stay outside the pack folder. site build refuses a pack that contains a holdout path.

items.title: Building the site
items.text:
symbolon site build packs --out site-registry [--key publisher.key] [--base-url https://…/registry]

For each pack, it validates the latest version (the build fails if any pack is invalid) and writes:

index.json                                 every pack: id, version, title, license, digest, tarball sha256, summary, files
llms.txt                                   one line per pack, for agents
packs/<owner>/<name>/
  latest.tar.gz                            the pack folder, byte-identical on every build
  latest.sha256                            sha256 of the tarball
  latest.sig.json                          with --key: a DSSE envelope over {pack, version, digest, tarball_sha256}
  pack.md                                  the whole pack in one Markdown file
  llms.txt                                 the pack's files, for agents
  files/…                                  every file of the pack, raw

The pack digest is the contract framing (CONTRACT_FORMAT.md) over the pack folder with the header symbolon-pack-v1\n.

Rendered previews and search pages are a later step (an Astro site over these files).

items.title: Pulling a pack
items.text:
symbolon pull acme/invoice-desk [--registry URL-or-folder] [--dest DIR] [--trust publisher.pub]

pull takes no version: the registry serves only the latest. It downloads the tarball, checks its sha256 against latest.sha256 and index.json, unpacks it, and checks the unpacked folder's digest against index.json. With --trust, it also requires a valid signature from that public key over the same digest and sha256. The registry defaults to $SYMBOLON_REGISTRY, or the kausalflow site.

An agent that only needs to read a pack can fetch packs/<owner>/<name>/pack.md instead and skip unpacking.

items.title: CLI reference
items.text:
Every command prints a ✓ or ✗ line per check and exits 0 on success, 1 on failure. Commands that print a report accept --json.

Command What it does init Scaffold a contract that passes validate out of the box validate Check a contract's structure, schema drift, examples, reference, spec vacuity and mutants; print the digest schema Regenerate schema/*.json from schema.py test Run a contract's spec against an implementation digest Print a contract's content digest impl-init Write an implementation manifest pinned to a contract's digest keygen Create this runner's Ed25519 signing key attest Run the spec in a sandbox and write a signed attestation verify Check an attestation's signature, trust and digests; optionally reproduce it diff Run several builds on one input pool and measure where they disagree extract Have a coding agent draft a spec pack from an existing product, then check the draft replicate Hand a pack to outside coding agents, then test, attest and diff their builds pack validate Check a spec pack's brief, assumptions and obligations pack init Scaffold a spec pack that passes pack validate out of the box site build Write the static registry for the latest version of every pack pull Download a pack from the registry, check it, and unpack it mutants Show which checks kill which mutants, and the kill rate canary plant Copy a contract for a builder with one example changed to contradict the spec canary check Tell whether a build followed the spec or was fitted to the planted example flag Report a part of the spec that contradicts itself, instead of coding around it

items.title: init
items.text:
symbolon init CONTRACT_ID [--root contracts] [--author you@example.com]

Creates <root>/<namespace>/<name>/versions/1/ with every required file and a reference implementation. CONTRACT_ID looks like namespace/name: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Fails if the directory exists.

items.title: validate
items.text:
symbolon validate PATH [--json]

Runs the checks listed in What symbolon validate checks and, if all pass, prints namespace/name@version sha256:<hex>. Contract code runs in a separate isolated Python process.

items.title: schema
items.text:
symbolon schema PATH

Writes schema/input.json and schema/output.json from the Input and Output models in schema.py.

items.title: test
items.text:
symbolon test PATH IMPL [--json]

Runs every example and property of the contract at PATH against IMPL, which is an implementation directory with symbolon-impl.toml or a single Python file. Failing properties print hypothesis's minimal failing case. This runs locally without a sandbox and signs nothing; use attest for evidence.

items.title: digest
items.text:
symbolon digest PATH

Prints sha256:<hex> for a contract directory. See Digest for exactly what it covers.

items.title: impl-init
items.text:
symbolon impl-init IMPL_DIR --contract CONTRACT_DIR [--entrypoint impl.py] [--author ...] [--license Apache-2.0]

Creates IMPL_DIR if needed and writes symbolon-impl.toml pinned to the contract's current digest. For implementations in other languages, edit the manifest to language = "command" and set command; see Implementations in other languages.

items.title: keygen
items.text:
symbolon keygen [--out ~/.config/symbolon/runner.key]

Creates an Ed25519 key for this runner. The public key is written next to it as runner.pub. Share the .pub with anyone who should trust your attestations.

items.title: attest
items.text:
symbolon attest CONTRACT IMPL [-o attestation.json] [--key ~/.config/symbolon/runner.key] [--sandbox auto|container|process]

Copies the contract and implementation into a fresh directory, checks that the implementation pins this contract's digest, runs the spec in a sandbox, and writes a signed in-toto attestation. Exits 0 if the result is PASSED. auto uses the container sandbox when Docker is reachable and the process sandbox otherwise. See Sandboxes.

items.title: verify
items.text:
symbolon verify ATTESTATION [--trust KEY.pub ...] [--contract DIR] [--impl DIR] [--rerun] [--key ...] [--sandbox ...]
Option Checks (none) The signature is valid and the statement is well-formed --trust The signer is one of these keys. Repeat for several --contract, --impl The attestation's digests match your local copies --rerun Runs the spec again here and compares every check's outcome. Needs --contract and --impl

items.title: diff
items.text:
symbolon diff CONTRACT IMPL IMPL... [--reference NAME] [--pool FILE ...] [--realistic FILE]
              [--mutations 500] [--property-cases 50] [--search 300] [--seed 0]
              [--weight NAME=W ...] [--severity TIER=W ...] [--max-ambiguity X]
              [--top 5] [-o report.json] [--json]

Runs every implementation on the same inputs: the contract's examples, inputs recorded from its property generators, mutated copies of both, any --pool files, and further mutations near each disagreement. It reports pairwise distances, the ambiguity of the ensemble with a 95% interval, behaviour classes, and the ways the builds split, largest first, each with a shrunk witness input and the obligations it traces to. Each IMPL is PATH or NAME=PATH; the name defaults to the build directory (rebuilds/go-1/search-query is go-1).

Option Effect --reference Compare this implementation (the original product) with every build, but leave it out of the ensemble --realistic A pool drawn to look like real use, reported as a separate estimate --weight Ensemble weight of a build, default 1 --severity Cost of each disagreement tier: crash, value, format (default 1, 1, 0.1) --max-ambiguity Exit 1 when the estimate is above this, for CI

Like test, it runs implementations in this process's environment, not a sandbox. See Measuring ambiguity.

items.title: extract
items.text:
symbolon extract SOURCE --pack NAMESPACE/PRODUCT [--root packs] [--version 1]
                 [--agent COMMAND] [--hint TEXT] [--rounds 2] [--timeout 3600] [--no-oracle]

Hands SOURCE to an external coding agent, which drafts ROOT/NAMESPACE/PRODUCT/versions/VERSION/ plus an oracle adapter per component and a REVIEW.md. The draft is then checked: the pack validates, every component validates, and the original product passes every component through its adapter. Failures go back to the agent for another round, up to --rounds runs in all. Component digests in symbolon-pack.toml are filled in for the agent. Symbolon never changes SOURCE.

Option Effect --agent The agent command; defaults to $SYMBOLON_AGENT, then Claude Code headless --hint Extra guidance for the agent, such as which parts of the product to cover --no-oracle Skip the oracle check, for products whose code cannot be called from an adapter

See Extracting a pack.

items.title: replicate
items.text:
symbolon replicate PACK [--agent NAME=COMMAND ...] [--builds 2] [--component NAME ...]
                   [--reference DIR] [--holdout DIR] [--holdout-seed N] [--holdout-scale 5]
                   [--attest | --no-attest] [--key PATH] [--sandbox auto] [--jobs 1]
                   [--agent-timeout 3600] [--prompt FILE] [--pool FILE ...]
                   [--mutations 500] [--property-cases 50] [--search 300] [--seed 0]
                   [--max-ambiguity X] [-o replication] [--json]

Gives a builder's copy of the pack at PACK to an outside coding agent once per build, then attests every component of every build, runs the holdout, and runs diff per component across the builds that passed. Symbolon does not build anything itself. Writes the builds, agent logs, attestations, diff reports and replication.json into the -o directory, which must not exist.

Option Effect --agent The agent command, NAME=COMMAND or a bare COMMAND named after its program; repeat for several, and builds take turns. Default $SYMBOLON_AGENT, then Claude Code headless --reference A directory with one implementation per component, such as a pack's oracle/: compared with every build, not part of the ensemble --holdout A directory of <component>.jsonl examples the builders never see, run with --holdout-seed and --holdout-scale times the property cases --no-attest Test each build instead of attesting it; no runner key needed --jobs How many agents run at once --prompt A prompt template instead of the default; $pack, $build and $components are filled in --pool, --mutations, --property-cases, --search, --seed Passed to diff

Exits 1 when a build fails a component or its holdout, or a component's ambiguity is above --max-ambiguity. The agent runs with your permissions, outside the sandbox. See Replicating a pack.

items.title: pack validate
items.text:
symbolon pack validate PATH [--json]

PATH is the pack directory holding symbolon-pack.toml. Checks the manifest, component digests, BRIEF.md sections, assumptions and obligations, then reports obligations by status and source. It does not run contract code; run validate on each component for that. See What symbolon pack validate checks.

items.title: mutants
items.text:
symbolon mutants PATH [--mutants DIR] [--json]

Runs the spec against each mutant in PATH/mutants/, or in DIR (useful for measuring a contract without changing its digest), and lists the checks that kill each one. Ends with the checks that kill no mutant and the kill rate. Exits 1 if a mutant survives without SURVIVES. See Mutants.

items.title: canary plant
items.text:
symbolon canary plant PATH OUT [--seed N] [--record FILE]

Copies the contract to OUT without reference/ and mutants/, and changes one example's expected output (chosen by --seed) to a value that still matches the output schema but contradicts the spec. Writes a private record, by default OUT.canary.json, next to the copy. Give the copy to a builder and keep the record. An honest build fails exactly that example.

items.title: canary check
items.text:
symbolon canary check RECORD IMPL [--contract PATH] [--flags FILE] [--json]

Runs the finished build on the canary input. The outcome is gamed if it returns the planted output (the build was fitted to the examples), honest if it returns what the spec requires, and other otherwise. Also reports whether the builder flagged the canary example in symbolon-flags.jsonl next to the build. Exits 1 only for gamed. In a replication, drop gamed builds from the convergence evidence.

items.title: flag
items.text:
symbolon flag REF REASON [--dir BUILD_DIR]

Appends {"ref", "reason", "flagged_at"} to BUILD_DIR/symbolon-flags.jsonl. REF is an obligation id, a check in pack form (search-query#example:40, search-query#test_name), or a bare example:<line>. Builders run this when an example and the description, or two checks, disagree, then build the reading they think is right. The flags file is part of the build directory, so it is covered by the implementation's digest.

items.title: pack init
items.text:
symbolon pack init PACK_ID [--dir spec] [--author you@example.com]

Creates a pack folder (by default spec/, next to your code) with a manifest, BRIEF.md, a placeholder open obligation, a placeholder assumption, components/ and AGENTS.md. Fails if the folder exists and is not empty. See Pack registry.

items.title: site build
items.text:
symbolon site build [REGISTRY=packs] [--out site-registry] [--key KEY] [--base-url URL]

Validates the latest version of every pack under REGISTRY and writes index.json, llms.txt, and each pack's tarball, sha256, pack.md, llms.txt and raw files. With --key, signs each pack. Fails if any pack is invalid or contains holdout files. See Pack registry.

items.title: pull
items.text:
symbolon pull PACK_ID [--registry URL-or-folder] [--dest DIR] [--trust PUBKEY]

Downloads the latest version of a pack, checks the tarball's sha256 and the unpacked pack's digest against the registry, and with --trust the publisher's signature, then unpacks it into DEST (default ./<name>). See Pack registry.

items.title: Contract
items.text:
A contract is a versioned, content-addressed statement of what a piece of software must do. In the first vertical, a capability contract is a directory:

File Role symbolon.toml Manifest: id, version, prose description, entrypoint, what the implementation may touch, spec budget schema.py and schema/*.json The interface: pydantic Input and Output models, and the language-neutral JSON Schema generated from them examples.jsonl Concrete cases: an input and either the exact output or the error it must raise properties.py Hypothesis properties that must hold for generated inputs reference/impl.py Optional reference implementation, used only as an oracle during validation

The prose description and the checks are two halves of one spec. The checks are what an implementation is held to; the description tells a builder, human or AI, what the checks mean.

A contract is valid only if its spec is not vacuous: its properties must reject an implementation that always raises and one that always returns a constant. A spec that cannot tell those apart from a real implementation is not a spec.

items.title: Digest
items.text:
A contract's identity is the SHA-256 digest of its files, nothing else. Timestamps and permissions are excluded, so the same contract has the same digest on every machine. namespace/name@version is only an alias. Any change to a contract's files changes its digest, and any change to its schema or spec should bump its version.

Implementations have digests too, computed the same way over their source, manifest and lockfile. The same code with different dependency pins is a different implementation.

items.title: Implementation
items.text:
An implementation is any code that claims to satisfy a contract. It is pinned to one contract digest in its symbolon-impl.toml. It exchanges only plain JSON values, so any tool or model can write one without importing Symbolon:

  • Python: a function, normally run(input: dict) -> dict, that raises ValueError on invalid input.
  • Any other language: a program that reads one JSON input per line on stdin and writes {"output": ...} or {"error": {...}} per line.

Implementations are disposable. The contract and the evidence about it are what last.

items.title: Attestation
items.text:
An attestation is signed evidence that one implementation passed or failed one contract's spec, in a recorded sandbox and environment, on a given runner. It is an in-toto Statement with the Test Result predicate, in a DSSE envelope signed with the runner's Ed25519 key. It names the contract digest, the implementation digest and an environment digest, and lists every check by name.

Two separate questions apply to any attestation:

  • Is it genuine? The signature verifies against the embedded public key.
  • Do I trust it? The key is one you accept, passed with --trust. Better still, verify --rerun reproduces the run locally.

items.title: Spec pack
items.text:
A spec pack is a product-level contract, packaged so a builder can rebuild the product in their own stack. It holds:

  • BRIEF.md: purpose, non-goals, priorities, and who resolves gaps.
  • assumptions/: facts about the world a builder may rely on.
  • obligations.toml: the decisions a build must keep, each decided, default or open, and each tied to the checks that pin it down.
  • components/: ordinary capability contracts.

Packs are meant to be minimal. They don't spell out what any good builder would do anyway; they hold the points where good builders would choose differently and the publisher would reject one choice. Most obligations are found by replication: give the pack to independent builders, compare their builds, and turn each disagreement into an obligation with a check. The lightkone pilot is the first worked example.

items.title: How they fit
items.text:
flowchart LR
  P[Spec pack] -->|lists by digest| C[Contract]
  I[Implementation] -->|pins| C
  R[Runner key] -->|signs| A[Attestation]
  A -->|names| C
  A -->|names| I
  V[Verifier] -->|checks or reruns| A

items.title: Symbolon — Product Design Document
items.text:
Status: Draft v0.3 (formerly Strand) Date: 2026-10-21 One-liner: Trustable contracts between agents: a commitment anyone can check, backed by evidence anyone can verify. Software capabilities are the first vertical.

The name. A symbolon was an ancient Greek token broken in two. Each party kept one half, and matching the halves proved the agreement. It is also the root of the word "symbol." Here, the contract is one half and the evidence that someone kept it is the other.

items.title: Changes since v0.2
items.text:
• Vision broadened. Contracts are now commitments between any parties, such as agents, software, services, and the humans they act for. Software capability contracts, the whole of v0.2, become the first vertical and the MVP (sections 1, 3, 4, 9).
  • One general model. Every contract kind uses the same primitives: parties, obligations, evidence, ledger, trust set, and counterexample. Only how the evidence is collected differs by kind (4.2, 4.3).
  • Product contracts and a business model. Specs and conformance suites become something you can sell, including to enterprises, while attestations stay public and unbuyable (6, 12).
  • Spec lifecycle and AI authoring protocol. Authors extract a spec from software they built. Users find, download, and fork it, and AI revises it under an enforced authoring protocol. Only a human key publishes (6.5, 6.6).
  • Governance section. This covers who stores contracts, who may change them, and how disputes resolve (8).
  • Standards reuse. Attestations use the in-toto format and Sigstore-style signing and transparency instead of a custom format (7).
  • Renamed. "Strand" collides with AWS Strands Agents.

items.title: 1. Summary
items.text:
Agents increasingly act for people and for each other. They call tools, run code they generated, hire other agents, and spend money on someone's behalf. Each of these is an implicit promise: this tool parses dates correctly, this agent will only touch the files I allowed, this service deletes my data after 30 days. Today none of those promises is written down in a checkable form, and none leaves verifiable evidence that it was kept.

Symbolon makes them explicit. A contract is a versioned, content-addressed statement of obligations between parties. An attestation is signed evidence that a specific party met those obligations in a specific case. A public ledger accumulates attestations and verified violations, so trust is earned from a record rather than asserted. Parties agree on contract digests, not on code, vendors, or reputations.

The first vertical is software capabilities. Here the obligations can be checked before execution by running a spec against an implementation in a sandbox. That is the most testable kind of promise, and it is where agents already rebuild things constantly.

items.title: 2. Problem
items.text:
Promises between agents are implicit. When agent A delegates to agent B, uses tool C, or relies on service D, the expectations are buried in prompts, docs, or terms of service. They cannot be compared, checked, or enforced.

There is no portable track record. An agent, a tool, or an implementation that behaved well yesterday leaves no evidence a stranger can verify today. Code generated fresh for each call has no history at all.

Coordination fails silently. Two agents interoperate only if they agree on behavior. When nobody declares that behavior, divergence stays invisible until something breaks.

Single points of trust are fragile. Ecosystems that depend on one implementation or one vendor inherit its failures, as in the left-pad incident or a compromised package. Contracts with many independently attested implementations do not.

Existing pieces each cover a slice. Tool and MCP registries cover discovery. Pact covers API contracts between services. SLSA, in-toto, and Sigstore cover build provenance. Tessl covers specs as the source of code. None of them combines a checkable obligation, independent evidence, and a public record of violations for agent-to-agent trust.

items.title: 3. Thesis
items.text:
What can be regenerated cheaply, like code, glue, and even whole agents, should be treated as disposable. What cannot be regenerated is access (credentials, legal agreements), state (data, histories), and track record (evidence that promises were kept). The durable asset is the promise and its evidence.

Trust between agents should therefore rest on three things: a precise promise, evidence that does not depend on trusting the party making the promise, and a public record of every verified violation.

items.title: 4.1 Primitives
items.text: Primitive What it is Contract Immutable, content-addressed set of obligations. It has roles (who promises and who relies), an interface, and a spec saying how each obligation is checked. Party Anything that can hold a key and take a role: an implementation, an agent, a service, a runner, a human principal. Obligation A checkable predicate. Example: "for every valid input, output matches the schema and properties"; "no network call outside the declared hosts"; "every write emits an audit event". Evidence / attestation A signed statement that a party met (or violated) obligations in a specific case, in in-toto format. Ledger The append-only record per contract and per party: attestations, verified counterexamples, deprecations, successor links. Trust set The verifier keys a caller accepts evidence from. Counterexample A concrete, reproducible case where a party violated an obligation. It is the only accepted form of complaint.

items.title: 4.2 Contract kinds
items.text:
All kinds share the primitives. They differ in when and how evidence is produced, and that sets the order of the roadmap.

Kind Example Evidence Verifiability Phase Capability Parse dates across locales Pre-execution: spec run against implementation in sandbox Strong, reproducible 1 (MVP) Product A full app with features, security and audit requirements Pre-execution: composed capability contracts plus end-to-end acceptance, security, and audit suites Strong for what is tested 2 Interaction Agent A and agent B exchange messages in a defined protocol Recorded transcripts checked against the protocol, both parties co-signing Medium 3 Mandate Agent acts for a human within scope, spend, and data limits Runtime receipts from an enforcing gateway, plus audit Medium; depends on the enforcement point 3 Service Hosted service promises data retention, latency, uptime Runtime monitoring by third-party verifiers Weaker; observational 4

The rule for ordering: start where evidence is strongest and the cost of a wrong verdict is lowest. Earn the right to the harder kinds with a working counterexample loop.

items.title: 4.3 Evidence strength
items.text:
Not all evidence is equal, so attestations declare their kind and callers weigh them:

  1. Reproducible: any verifier given the same digests gets the same result. Capability and product contracts with pure specs.
  2. Co-signed: both parties sign the same record. Interaction contracts.
  3. Enforced: a trusted enforcement point signs what it allowed and blocked. Mandate contracts.
  4. Observed: a third party saw it happen, but cannot replay it. Service contracts and anything with network access.

items.title: 4.4 Ranking
items.text:
Wherever several parties can fulfil the same contract, ranking uses only published evidence:

  1. number of distinct trusted verifiers that attested the party;
  2. verified counterexamples against it (fewer is better);
  3. age of its first trusted attestation.

Raw attestation count is never an input, because it is free to inflate. There is no sponsored placement and no opaque score, and money never buys evidence.

items.title: 5. First vertical: software capability contracts
items.text: This section carries v0.2 forward. Section numbers in brackets refer to v0.2, where the detail is unchanged.

items.title: 5.1 Capability contract
items.text:
Identified by digest: SHA-256 over a deterministic archive of the contract directory. The alias is namespace/name@version. Namespaces are bound to a publisher key, and versions are integers; any change to the schema or spec bumps the version.

It contains a JSON Schema interface (canonical; pydantic is authoring sugar), an entrypoint signature (MVP: synchronous run(input) -> output), and a behavioral spec. The spec has three parts: examples as data, derandomized hypothesis properties, and an optional reference implementation used only as an oracle. It also declares external requirements (credentials by name, network hosts, state, permissions), a regenerability class, and provenance including the license. [v0.2 4.1]

items.title: 5.2 Implementation
items.text: A directory of source code, a manifest naming the target contract digest, and a pinned lockfile. Its identity is the digest of all three. Generated implementations record the generator in the manifest. [v0.2 4.2]

items.title: 5.3 Attestation and reproducibility
items.text: The runner executes the spec against the implementation in a sandbox: no network unless declared, resource limits, a pinned environment digest, and derandomized tests. Both the implementation and the contract's test code are untrusted and run inside the sandbox. The result is an in-toto attestation signed by the runner. Each attestation carries the contract and implementation digests, test results with seed and budget, a resource profile, the environment digest, and runner and submitter identity. [v0.2 4.3, 4.4]

items.title: 5.4 Regenerability
items.text:
• Disposable: any trusted-attested implementation is acceptable, and callers may regenerate at will.
  • Pinned: callers converge on one implementation digest chosen by ranking; generation is allowed only when none exists.
  • Sovereign: reserved. It is effectively a service contract and comes in phase 4. [v0.2 4.7]

items.title: 5.5 Resolution
items.text: resolve(contract, version) returns a local path plus the backing attestation. Loading the code is a separate, explicit step under the caller's policy. For disposable contracts with nothing attested, resolution generates an implementation, attests it, and caches it. Expected latency is under a second when cached, and tens of seconds to minutes for generate-then-attest. [v0.2 4.8]

items.title: 6. Product contracts (phase 2)
items.text: A product contract specifies a whole application well enough that any capable AI can build it, a buyer can customize it, and anyone can check the result. The motivating case is a project like lightkone: rebuilding it from scratch today takes many rounds of human iteration.

items.title: 6.1 Structure
items.text:
• Composition: a graph of capability contracts, referenced by digest.
  • Acceptance suite: end-to-end scenarios over the composed product.
  • Security suite: a full role × action authorization matrix, with each cell tested. It also includes input fuzzing, a declared network allowlist checked in the sandbox, a dependency policy, and a threat model where each threat maps to at least one test.
  • Audit suite: required audit events as testable obligations. Example: "every state-changing request emits an event with actor, action, target and timestamp."
  • Non-functional notes: UX, performance, and operations guidance that is not yet testable, clearly marked as such.

items.title: 6.2 Making a spec replicable by any AI
items.text:
A spec is only as good as its weakest untested behavior. The method for closing the gap:

  1. Two or three different AI systems build independently from the spec.
  2. Each build runs the full suites.
  3. Wherever builds pass but behave differently, the spec is missing an obligation. Add a test that pins the intended behavior.
  4. Repeat until independent builds converge.

The convergence result is published evidence of spec quality: the number of independent builds that pass, and the remaining known divergences.

items.title: 6.3 What a spec cannot guarantee
items.text: UX quality, performance under real load, and novel vulnerabilities outside the tested threat model. A product contract states this plainly, and passing it means "meets every tested obligation", nothing more.

items.title: 6.4 Customization
items.text: Buyers fork with lineage. Their changes become new contract versions, and conformance to the parent contract's suites can still be checked and attested.

items.title: 6.5 Spec lifecycle: extract, find, download, revise, publish
items.text:
The loop a person runs, with AI doing most of the work:

  1. Extract. An author points Symbolon at software they built. An AI reads the code and observes its behavior, then proposes a product contract: the composition, the schemas, the examples, and the acceptance, security, and audit suites. The original software is the reference oracle. The spec must pass against it, and it must fail the vacuity stubs. The author reviews it and publishes.
  2. Find. Users search the registry by capability, contract kind, and evidence. Results show convergence results, counterexample counts, lineage, and license, never a popularity score.
  3. Download. pull fetches the contract by digest with its suites and evidence, and verifies signatures locally. Any AI tool can build from it, and the build is checked with attest.
  4. Revise. A user forks and asks an AI to change the spec, for example to add a feature or tighten security. The AI must follow the authoring protocol (6.6).
  5. Publish. The new version passes validate, and the convergence loop if it is a product contract. It carries a changelog and lineage to its parent, and is signed by the human owner of the namespace. AI may draft and check a version, but only a human key can publish it.

items.title: 6.6 Authoring protocol for AI
items.text:
The guidelines AI follows are themselves a published, versioned contract: the authoring protocol. They are machine-readable rules, not prose advice. Symbolon serves it to any AI as an MCP server or agent skill, and validate enforces it, so a version that breaks the rules cannot be published whichever AI wrote it.

The protocol requires that:

  • every new or changed behavior comes with at least one example or property that pins it down;
  • a revision never deletes an existing test without a recorded reason, and deleting one makes the change breaking;
  • every security-relevant feature updates the authorization matrix and threat model;
  • every state-changing feature declares its audit events;
  • the changelog states, per change, whether behavior changed, and which tests prove it;
  • the spec passes against the reference implementation and fails the vacuity stubs;
  • for product contracts, the convergence loop (6.2) ran, and its result is attached.

Because the protocol is a contract, it has its own versions and its own counterexamples. If a spec that followed it still turns out to be weak, that counts against the protocol, and its next version tightens the rules.

items.title: 7. Architecture
items.text:
Component Role Contract store Immutable contracts addressed by digest, with aliases. A git repository at first. Verifiers Produce evidence. For capability and product contracts, these are sandboxed attestation runners. Later kinds add transcript checkers, enforcement gateways, and monitors. Each verifier has a published key. Ledger Append-only record of attestations and counterexamples. It mirrors to a Sigstore-style transparency log so that history cannot be rewritten quietly. Resolver Selects a party for a contract using the caller's trust set and the ranking rules. For capability contracts, it falls back to generation when allowed. Counterexample service Accepts violation reports, replays them through a verifier, and records the result.

Formats reuse standards: JSON Schema for interfaces, in-toto statements for attestations, Ed25519 or Sigstore keyless signing, and SHA-256 content addressing. The novelty is in what gets signed and how the record is used, not in the cryptography.

items.title: 8. Governance
items.text:
Storage. Publishers sign contracts with their namespace key and push them to the registry. Contracts are content-addressed, so anyone may mirror them, and a mirror is verifiable. Storage is not a trust point.

Change. Only the namespace key holder can publish new versions. Nobody can amend a published contract.

Disputes. The spec is the only arbiter.

  • If a counterexample makes the current spec fail, it is objectively valid. It is recorded against the party, and against the verifier that attested it.
  • If the spec passes it, it is a proposal. The author may adopt it in a new version, or anyone may fork with it. Adoption follows evidence.
  • Symbolon does not adjudicate intent.

Registry operator. Handles only namespace disputes (squatting, abandoned namespaces) and legal takedowns, under a published policy. Every action is logged in the ledger. Federation (section 15) removes the single operator.

items.title: 9. Users
items.text:
Phase 1: agent developers who want capabilities without hard dependencies; agents as runtime callers of resolve; contract authors. Phase 2: product teams and enterprises that buy or commission product contracts to build and customize applications with their own AI tools. Phase 3 and later: operators of multi-agent systems who need agents to keep promises to each other and to the humans they act for.

Non-users for now: end consumers and anyone whose primary need is credential management.

items.title: 10. Product surfaces
items.text:
• CLI and Python package (phase 1): init, validate (including the vacuity check), attest, resolve, publish, report, and later fork. [v0.2 6.1]
  • Registry: a git repository first, with layout contracts/, ledger/, implementations/, attestations/, verifiers/. A hosted index and API come later. [v0.2 6.2]
  • Runtime library: resolve() with an in-process cache, a configurable trust set, and an optional local runner. [v0.2 6.3]
  • Contract studio (phase 2): tooling for authoring product contracts and running the multi-AI convergence loop in 6.2. Adds extract (spec from existing software), search, and pull (6.5).
  • Authoring protocol server (phase 2): an MCP server or agent skill that hands any AI the authoring protocol and checks drafts against it (6.6).

items.title: 11. MVP scope (phase 1)
items.text:
Unchanged from v0.2 section 8:

  1. Contract format, init, validate, and three seed contracts (core/date-parse, core/csv-to-records, core/unit-convert).
  2. Implementation format and attest with a container sandbox and in-toto output.
  3. End-to-end slice: one implementation attested on two machines with identical results.
  4. Git registry, publish, lookup-only resolve with a trust set.
  5. Generate-then-attest for disposable contracts.
  6. 10 to 20 pure seed contracts; counterexample reporting.

Success: an outside agent resolves a seed contract and gets a working implementation; a third-party runner reproduces the attestation; at least one outside developer chooses resolve over in-house generation and can say why.

items.title: 12. Business model
items.text:
• Free: public contracts, public attestations, the open-source CLI and runner.
  • Paid, phase 1 to 2: private registries and a hosted canonical runner (metered attestation).
  • Paid, phase 2: product contracts. Buyers pay for the conformance suites, convergence evidence, and maintained updates. The prose spec copies as easily as code; the suites and the ongoing record are the product.
  • Enterprise: private namespaces, commissioned product contracts, on-premises runners.

Invariant: evidence is never for sale. Ranking stays purely evidence-based and fully published, regardless of who pays for what.

items.title: 13. Non-goals
items.text: Symbolon is not a credential manager, a package manager replacement, an agent framework, a general code-generation product, or a legal contract platform. It does not host long-running customer services. It does not verify properties beyond what a contract's spec states. Payments between agents are out of scope; mandate contracts may describe spend limits, but Symbolon does not move money.

items.title: 14. Risks and open questions
items.text:
• The spec is the real product. Weak specs attest bad implementations. Mitigations: the vacuity check, reference oracles, the counterexample loop, and multi-AI convergence (6.2).
  • Tests do not cover security. State it plainly. Product contracts narrow the gap through explicit security suites, but cannot close it.
  • Malicious contracts and verifiers. Contract code runs sandboxed. Verifiers are weighted by trust set and penalized by verified counterexamples.
  • Scope creep. The broader vision is a direction, not the MVP. Phase gates: move to the next contract kind only after the previous one shows a working counterexample loop and outside adoption.
  • Weaker evidence in later phases. Interaction, mandate, and service contracts rely on co-signed, enforced, or observed evidence. Callers must see the evidence strength, never a single green check.
  • Spec piracy. Specs are easy to copy. The paid value is the maintained suites, the evidence, and the updates, so treat the prose as marketing.
  • Demand. Agents may prefer to generate and test locally. The MVP demand test checks this before anything else scales.
  • Name. Trademark and domain checks still to do (see section 16).

items.title: 15. Longer-term direction
items.text: Contracts that compose across kinds. For example, a product contract whose deployment carries a mandate contract for the agents operating it. Other directions: cross-language implementations, record/replay so networked capabilities become reproducible, federation of registries and verifiers across organizations, and a standard way for agents to present their ledger history to each other before collaborating.

items.title: 16. Naming
items.text:
"Strand" is retired because of AWS Strands Agents. Symbolon was chosen on 2026-10-21. Quick web checks on 2026-10-21 (not trademark or domain searches):

Name Meaning Collision found Symbolon (chosen 2026-10-21) Greek token split between two parties; matching halves proves the agreement None notable in software or AI Chirograph Medieval deed written twice on one sheet and cut apart; the matching cut proves authenticity None in software Syngraph Greek for a written contract signed by both parties None notable Tessera Roman token of a pact Taken: Google's transparency-log library, same space Countersign Second signature confirming a first Taken: an existing npm MCP package Warrant Guarantee Taken: an authorization startup Surety Guarantee of another's obligation Crowded by surety-bond insurance software

items.title: 17. Glossary
items.text: Contract. An immutable, content-addressed set of obligations between roles, with a spec saying how each is checked. Party. A key-holding participant: implementation, agent, service, verifier, or human principal. Obligation. A checkable predicate within a contract. Attestation. Signed evidence that a party met or violated obligations, with a declared evidence strength. Evidence strength. Reproducible, co-signed, enforced, or observed. Ledger. The append-only record of attestations and verified counterexamples. Counterexample. A reproducible case of a violated obligation; the only accepted form of complaint. Trust set. The verifier keys a caller accepts. Capability / product / interaction / mandate / service contract. The contract kinds, in roadmap order. Resolve. For capability contracts: return an attested implementation, generating one if permitted. Vacuity check. Validation proving a spec rejects trivial implementations.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Symbolon needs Python 3.11 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/kausalflow/symbolon
cd symbolon
pip install -e ".[dev]"
symbolon --help

Attestations run in a sandbox. The container sandbox needs a reachable Docker daemon; the process sandbox needs unprivileged user namespaces (unshare -rn). symbolon test and symbolon validate need neither.

items.title: Check a seed contract
items.text:
The repository ships three seed contracts under contracts/core/.

symbolon validate contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1

✓ required files present
✓ symbolon.toml is valid  core/date-parse@1
✓ schema.py defines Input and Output
✓ schema/*.json matches schema.py
✓ examples.jsonl is valid  14 examples
✓ properties.py collects  7 properties
✓ spec passes against reference implementation
✓ vacuity: properties reject an implementation that always raises
✓ vacuity: properties reject an implementation that returns a constant

core/date-parse@1  sha256:...

The last line is the contract's identity: core/date-parse@1 is a human-readable alias for the digest.

items.title: Test implementations against it
items.text:
symbolon test contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 examples/impls/date-parse-strptime   # fails: too lenient
symbolon test contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 examples/impls/date-parse-strict     # passes

An implementation is a directory with a symbolon-impl.toml manifest, or for quick checks a single Python file that defines run(input: dict) -> dict. See Implementations and attestations.

items.title: Write your own contract
items.text:
symbolon init acme/shout                      # scaffold a contract that already validates
symbolon validate contracts/acme/shout/versions/1

init writes a complete, valid contract so you can change one file at a time and re-validate. The walkthrough in Writing a contract covers each file.

items.title: Sign and verify evidence
items.text:
symbolon keygen                                    # this runner's Ed25519 key
symbolon attest contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 examples/impls/date-parse-strict -o att.json
symbolon verify att.json --trust ~/.config/symbolon/runner.pub \
  --contract contracts/core/date-parse/versions/1 --impl examples/impls/date-parse-strict --rerun

attest exits 0 when the implementation passes. verify --rerun runs the spec again in your own sandbox and checks that every example and property has the same outcome, so you don't have to trust the original runner.

items.title: Run the tests
items.text:
pytest

Sandbox tests run for each sandbox available on the machine and are skipped otherwise.

items.title: Lightkone pilot
items.text:
The first spec pack built from a real product: lightkone, a static web app for keeping a personal library of research papers. The pack lives in packs/kausalflow/lightkone/.

Path What it is Ships to buyers versions/1/ The pack, version 1: BRIEF, AGENTS, assumptions, obligations, and eight component contracts yes oracle/ Publisher side: lightkone's own TypeScript bundled as command implementations, fixtures, example recorder, holdout, differential tester no rebuilds/python-1/ Milestone 1: an AI build in Python (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code) of the first three contracts no rebuilds/go-1/ Milestone 2: a second AI build in Go of all eight contracts, with its NOTES.md no attestations/ Signed evidence for both builds, plus the runner keys yes, as evidence

items.title: What the pack covers
items.text:
Component What it does lightkone/search-query@1 The search box: filters, words with accent folding, ranking, sort orders, and the trash rule lightkone/bibtex-import@1 Reading BibTeX from the common reference managers into paper drafts lightkone/bibtex-export@1 Writing a paper as the exact BibTeX entry lightkone writes, byte for byte lightkone/citation-key@1 Paperpile-style citation keys for new papers, unique within the library lightkone/pdf-filing@1 Where a paper's PDF goes, named the way Paperpile names it lightkone/library-merge@1 Merging two devices' edits to library.json without losing either lightkone/tidy@1 Finding duplicate papers and how to merge each group lightkone/library-file@1 Reading library.json and writing it back, with library.bib, byte for byte

symbolon pack validate packs/kausalflow/lightkone/versions/1 reports 63 obligations (all decided) and 4 assumptions, and every one of the components' 337 checks traces to an obligation.

items.title: Results (milestone 2)
items.text:
Five more contracts: citation-key, pdf-filing, library-merge, tidy, and library-file, the data contract for library.json itself (how lightkone reads it and writes it back, byte for byte, with library.bib). Contracts can now share sample data in fixtures/, including raw text files with {"$text": ...}; library-file ships three sample libraries.

Contract Checks lightkone Go rebuild Holdout (Go) Second runner lightkone/search-query@1 81 examples + 11 properties PASSED PASSED 101/101 reproduced both lightkone/bibtex-import@1 37 examples + 13 properties PASSED PASSED 56/56 reproduced both lightkone/bibtex-export@1 19 examples + 6 properties PASSED PASSED 28/28 reproduced both lightkone/citation-key@1 19 examples + 6 properties PASSED PASSED 28/28 reproduced both lightkone/pdf-filing@1 19 examples + 6 properties PASSED PASSED 28/28 reproduced both lightkone/library-merge@1 21 examples + 8 properties PASSED PASSED 31/31 reproduced both lightkone/tidy@1 21 examples + 5 properties PASSED PASSED 28/28 reproduced both lightkone/library-file@1 39 examples + 7 properties PASSED PASSED 54/54 reproduced both

How it went:

  1. Second build, second language. A fresh Claude Code session (Claude Opus 5.5, the same model as the Python build, with no access to it) got only versions/1/ and built all eight components in Go (standard library only), with lightkone, the oracle and the Python rebuild moved off the machine. It passed all eight contracts and all eight holdouts.
  2. Passing is not agreeing. oracle/differential.py sends the same generated inputs to lightkone and the Go build and reports every disagreement on inputs the contract accepts. On about 5,000 inputs, six contracts agreed completely. bibtex-import and search-query showed five real gaps that both the spec and the holdout had missed:
  3. a malformed BibTeX field skipped to a } ends the entry, but one skipped to a comma does not (the contract said the rest was always lost);
  4. "whitespace" means JavaScript's \s, including no-break space and U+2028;
  5. the arXiv URL match ignores case, so V3 and .PDF are stripped;
  6. year: terms that are not numbers do not count, and do not replace an earlier one;
  7. title sort is Unicode collation (localeCompare), not code-point order.
  8. Tightened and rebuilt. The contracts now state each rule, with 18 new examples recorded from lightkone. The Go builder revised from the new text alone (adding golang.org/x/text for collation) and passes. The differential test then found no disagreement on search-query within scope, and 11 in 2,000 heavily mutated BibTeX files, all deliberately broken input (unbalanced braces, a value starting with #); those are left for a later version.
  9. Evidence. Runner A attested lightkone and the Go build on all eight contracts; runner B re-ran all sixteen in fresh containers with identical outcomes. The Python build's milestone 1 attestations are kept: they are for the earlier digests of search-query and bibtex-import.

The pack now has 63 obligations, all decided. Four defaults that were lightkone bugs are fixed and decided: papers in the trash are left out of library.bib, and top-level keys of library.json that lightkone does not use are kept on save (lightkone#51); a user folder named in capitals (ML, 2019) is no longer taken for a Paperpile author folder unless it is an author's surname, and blank DOIs no longer match each other in tidy (lightkone#52). On 2026-10-24 kausalflow settled the last five: an empty journal no longer hides the booktitle as the venue, and a library.json saved by a newer lightkone is refused rather than read as version 1 (lightkone#53); a mistyped year: filter still filters nothing, title sort keeps Unicode collation, and import keeps JavaScript's whitespace set.

Two Symbolon bugs turned up and are fixed: examples containing U+2028 were split into two lines, and the container sandbox removed the execute bit, so no compiled implementation could run.

items.title: Results (milestone 1)
items.text:
Contract Checks lightkone (oracle) Python rebuild Holdout (rebuild) Second runner lightkone/search-query@1 71 examples + 11 properties PASSED PASSED 91/91 reproduced both lightkone/bibtex-import@1 28 examples + 13 properties PASSED PASSED 47/47 reproduced both lightkone/bibtex-export@1 19 examples + 6 properties PASSED PASSED 28/28 reproduced both
  1. Oracle check. Examples were recorded by running lightkone's own code through the command protocol. The properties were written from the description, and lightkone passed all of them.
  2. Replication. An AI builder got only versions/1/, with lightkone's source and the oracle moved off the machine. It passed all three contracts, then passed the holdout: a different property seed, 5× the generated cases, and 18 examples it never saw.
  3. Divergence found. Comparing the two builds on the builder's listed ambiguities found one real gap in how repeated year: filters combine. The contract now states the rule, with a property and two examples for it, and both builds pass it.
  4. Reproduction. A second runner key re-ran all six attestations in a fresh container, and every check had the same outcome.
  5. Kill rate. Plausible wrong versions of the rebuild live in examples/mutants/lightkone/, outside the pack so the component digests stay put. search-query rejects 8 of 9; the one survivor ignores a malformed year: term, which is exactly what the open obligation search.year-malformed leaves to the builder. bibtex-export rejects 7 of 7. bibtex-import rejects 7 of 8; the survivor reads a two-digit year like 99 as a number, which the description rules out but no check covers, so it is a gap for the next pack version.

items.title: Measuring the remaining ambiguity
items.text: symbolon diff turns the milestone 2 differential test into a command that works on any number of builds (see Measuring ambiguity). Run on search-query with lightkone as the reference and both rebuilds, it puts the Go build at distance 0 from lightkone. It finds the two rules milestone 2 tightened, search.year-malformed and search.title-sort-other, as the splits between the milestone 1 Python build and the other two. On bibtex-import, after the importer fix in kausalflow/lightkone#50, it finds no disagreement between lightkone and the Go build.

items.title: Re-running the evidence
items.text:
cd packs/kausalflow/lightkone
symbolon pack validate 1
symbolon verify attestations/search-query.go-1.json --trust attestations/runner-a.pub \
  --contract versions/1/components/search-query/versions/1 --impl rebuilds/go-1/search-query --rerun

The pack's own README.md has the full notes, including the three importer bugs the contracts found, now fixed in lightkone#50.

items.title: Seed contracts
items.text:
Three small contracts ship in contracts/core/. They are worked examples of the format and test fixtures for the tooling.

Contract Capability Examples Properties core/date-parse@1 Parse a date written in ISO, en-US, en-GB or de-DE conventions into an ISO 8601 date 14 7 core/csv-to-records@1 Parse RFC 4180 CSV with a header row into records keyed by header 14 5 core/csv-to-records@2 As version 1, and malformed quoting raises ValueError 17 5 core/unit-convert@1 Convert length, mass and temperature with the exact international factors 15 8

Each has six mutants in mutants/. date-parse kills all six. csv-to-records@1 kills five; the survivor accepts malformed quoting such as "x"y, which version 1's description never rules on. Version 2 settles it: text after a closing quote, or a quote never closed, raises ValueError, and all six mutants are killed. unit-convert kills five; the survivor uses binary floats, which the 1e-9 tolerance allows. symbolon mutants contracts/core/<name>/versions/1 shows the full matrix.

items.title: core/date-parse@1
items.text:
Day and month may omit leading zeros, except in ISO. The year is always four digits. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. Strings that don't match the locale's pattern, or that name a date that doesn't exist, raise ValueError.

Two implementations in examples/impls/ show what the properties are for. date-parse-strptime is the plausible one-shot version built on datetime.strptime. It passes most examples but accepts 2000-1-1 as ISO, which test_iso_requires_two_digit_month_and_day finds. date-parse-strict checks the string's shape with a regular expression first, and passes.

items.title: core/csv-to-records@1 and @2
items.text:
Quoted fields may contain the delimiter, newlines and doubled quotes. Rows end with LF or CRLF, and blank lines are skipped. Values are returned exactly as written, with no trimming or type conversion. A missing header, empty or duplicate header names, or a row with the wrong number of fields raise ValueError.

Version 2 adds one rule. Text after a field's closing quote ("x"y) or a quote that is never closed raises ValueError; a quote inside an unquoted field (x"y) is an ordinary character.

items.title: core/unit-convert@1
items.text: Length: mm, cm, m, km, in, ft, yd, mi. Mass: mg, g, kg, oz, lb. Temperature: C, F, K. Converting between dimensions, or a temperature below absolute zero, raises ValueError. Results are compared with a relative tolerance of 1e-9.

items.title: Extracting a pack
items.text:
