symbolon extract turns a product you already built into a draft spec pack. It follows design v0.5, sections 5.1 and 5.2: an AI reads the product and drafts a minimal pack, and the original product is the oracle the draft must pass.

Symbolon does not read code or write software itself. It hands that to a coding agent you already use, then checks what the agent leaves behind.

items.title: Run it
items.text:
symbolon extract ~/code/lightkone --pack kausalflow/lightkone \
  --hint "Cover search, BibTeX import and export, and the library file."

The agent works in packs/kausalflow/lightkone/ and may read the source, which Symbolon never changes. When it finishes you have:

Path What it is Ships versions/1/ The draft pack: BRIEF, AGENTS, assumptions, obligations, component contracts yes oracle/<name>/ An adapter per component that runs the original code as an implementation no REVIEW.md What you must confirm: non-goals, priorities, each default obligation and assumption, suspected bugs no .symbolon/ The prompt and each round's agent log no

items.title: What is checked
items.text:
After each agent run, extract fills in the component digests in symbolon-pack.toml and checks:

  1. symbolon pack validate passes on the draft.
  2. symbolon validate passes on every component.
  3. The original passes every component, through oracle/<name>/ (skip with --no-oracle).
  4. REVIEW.md exists.

If anything fails, the failures go back to the agent for another round, up to --rounds runs (default 2). A draft that still fails is left in place for you to fix by hand.

A draft that passes is a starting point, not a finished pack. The examples were recorded from the original, so they show what it does, including its bugs. The statuses are the agent's guesses: answer REVIEW.md, settle each default and open obligation, and then let replication show what the pack still leaves undecided (Measuring ambiguity).

items.title: Choosing the agent
items.text:
The agent is any command that reads a prompt on stdin, works in its current directory, and exits 0 when done. In order, extract uses:

  1. --agent "COMMAND"
  2. $SYMBOLON_AGENT
  3. Claude Code headless: claude -p --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep,Bash

The default lets the agent run shell commands without asking, since it must run symbolon and the product's code to record examples. Run it on a machine or container where that is acceptable.

The prompt is also written to a file. A command can name it as {prompt_file} and its working directory as {workdir}; the agent also gets SYMBOLON_PROMPT_FILE, SYMBOLON_WORKDIR, and SYMBOLON_EXTRA_DIRS (the source directory) in its environment. Claude Code is given the source with --add-dir.

For an agent that wants the prompt as an argument, wrap it in a script. Commands are split the way a shell would split them but are not run through a shell, so a script is also the place for $(...) and pipes:

cat > codex-agent.sh <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
exec codex exec --full-auto "$(cat "$SYMBOLON_PROMPT_FILE")"
SH
chmod +x codex-agent.sh
symbolon extract ./product --pack acme/product --agent ./codex-agent.sh

items.title: Measuring ambiguity
items.text: Passing a contract shows a build agrees with the spec on the cases the spec samples. Two builds that both pass can still behave differently. Each difference is a point the contract leaves undecided, whether or not anyone meant it to. symbolon diff finds these points and measures how much they cost. It follows the sufficiency test in The Probabilistic Minimal Reproduction Kit (sections 4 and 6.2).

items.title: Run it
items.text:
cd packs/kausalflow/lightkone
symbolon diff versions/1/components/search-query/versions/1 \
  oracle/search-query rebuilds/go-1/search-query rebuilds/python-1/search-query \
  --reference oracle -o diff-search-query.json

pool       1295 inputs (80 example, 718 property, 315 mutation, 182 search), 188 with a disagreement
ensemble   go-1  weight 1  no [generator] recorded
ensemble   python-1  weight 1  python  (built for another contract digest)
reference  oracle  (compared, not in the ensemble)
distance   oracle | go-1  0.0000
distance   oracle | python-1  0.1028
distance   go-1 | python-1  0.1028
ambiguity  0.1028  (95% 0.0865–0.1230; expected error ≥ 0.0514)
...
splits, largest first (3):
1. oracle, go-1 | python-1   95% of ambiguity, 127 inputs, value
   traces to  search.year-malformed
   witness    {"papers": [...], "query": "..."}
2. oracle, go-1 | python-1   4% of ambiguity, 55 inputs, format
   traces to  search.title-sort-other

The Python build is from milestone 1, before the year and title-sort rules were tightened, so diff finds those two rules again from the builds alone.

items.title: The input pool
items.text:
Source What it adds Examples Every example input Properties The inputs each property's generator produces (--property-cases per property) Mutations Copies of the above with a changed leaf, or a list item dropped, repeated or swapped (--mutations) --pool FILE Your own inputs, one JSON input or {"input": ...} per line Search More mutations of each disagreeing input, since a split is rarely found by one input alone (--search)

Only inputs the contract's Input accepts are used. Random generators rarely produce the rare combinations where readings differ. In the lightkone pilot, the year rule hid for that reason: no generated query had an exact year followed by a range. Mutation and search are there to find these.

The pool is not a sample of real use, so its estimate is biased towards the inputs the spec already thinks about. Pass --realistic FILE with inputs drawn from real use (exported libraries, logged queries) to get a separate estimate on that pool alone.

items.title: What the numbers mean
items.text:
• Distance between two builds: the share of inputs on which they disagree, weighted by severity. A crash (an output that breaks the schema, or a process that died) and a different value cost 1. A format difference costs 0.1: outputs that agree once case, spacing and list order are ignored. Change the costs with --severity.
  • Ambiguity: the expected distance between two builds drawn from the ensemble, with a bootstrap interval over inputs. Half of it is a lower bound on the expected error of a build, whatever the intended behaviour is. Disagreement is not the only source of error: builds can all agree on the same wrong reading, and that shows only against the reference, a holdout or mutants.
  • Behaviours: builds with identical outcomes on every input form one class. The Chao estimate guesses how many classes have not been seen yet. Both need more than a handful of builds to mean much.
  • Error vs reference: each build's distance to --reference, when there is one. The reference is not part of the ensemble, so the ambiguity does not need it.

items.title: Splits and the ambiguity map
items.text:
A split is one way the builds divide (oracle, go-1 | python-1) about one thing. That thing is the obligations whose checks the inputs came from, or the inputs' origin when nothing traces. Splits are ranked by their share of the ambiguity, so the first one is the question worth settling first. Each split has a witness, its smallest input, shrunk while the builds still split the same way.

"no obligation: a gap in the pack" means the inputs came from a --pool file or from checks no obligation lists. Settle it by adding an obligation with a check, or by marking the point open.

items.title: The ensemble
items.text:
The estimate is only as good as the builds behind it. One model tends to choose the same reading every time, so the builds should come from several model families and at least two languages. Record each build's model in its symbolon-impl.toml:

[generator]
model = "..."
family = "..."
language = "go"

--weight NAME=W gives a build more or less weight (default 1). The report's ensemble table records all of this next to the estimate.

items.title: Readings
items.text:
Builders should record the points where they chose between readings, in readings.toml next to the build. It goes in the implementation directory, or at the build root with a component on each entry:

[[reading]]
component = "search-query"
point = "Two year: terms in one query"
obligation = "search.year-last-wins"    # optional: the obligation it is about
considered = ["all must hold", "last wins"]
chosen = "last wins"

diff lists the points that two or more builds recorded and chose differently. These are often the splits the input pool has not found yet.

items.title: In CI
items.text:
symbolon diff CONTRACT build-a build-b --max-ambiguity 0.01

This exits 1 when the estimate is above the threshold. A contract change that raises the ambiguity is a regression of the contract, even if every check passes.

items.title: Replicating a pack
items.text: A pack is good enough when independent builders, given only the pack, make builds that pass it and behave the same. symbolon replicate runs that test. It does not write code. It hands the pack to outside coding agents, such as Claude Code, and then checks what they made, the way the lightkone pilots did by hand (design v0.5, section 5.3).

items.title: Run it
items.text:
symbolon keygen                                   # once: the runner key for attestations
cd packs/kausalflow/lightkone
symbolon replicate versions/1 --builds 3 \
  --agent claude="claude -p --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools Read,Write,Edit,Glob,Grep,Bash" \
  --agent other="my-agent --task-file {prompt_file}" \
  --reference oracle --holdout oracle/holdout -o replication-1

For each build, replicate:

  1. makes a work directory with the builder's copy of the pack in pack/ (without reference/ or mutants/) and an empty build/;
  2. runs the agent there with a prompt that says which components to build into build/<component>/, how to check them with symbolon test, and where to write NOTES.md, readings.toml and flags;
  3. re-pins each symbolon-impl.toml the agent wrote to the published contract digest (the builder's copy differs only by the files left out) and adds a [generator] section naming the agent, unless the agent wrote one;
  4. attests each component in a sandbox, so a passing build comes with signed evidence (--no-attest only tests it);
  5. runs the holdout when --holdout is given: a different property seed, --holdout-scale times the generated cases, and the publisher's <component>.jsonl examples, which the builder never saw.

Then, per component, it runs symbolon diff across the builds that passed, with --reference as the original product when there is one.

Builds take turns among the --agents, so --builds 3 with two agents makes claude-1, other-2 and claude-3. Different agent families make a better ensemble than one agent run three times, because they share fewer defaults.

items.title: Which agent runs
items.text:
Any command line that reads a prompt on stdin and works in its current directory. The prompt is also written to .symbolon/prompt.md, and {prompt_file} and {workdir} in the command are replaced by those paths, for agents that want them. Without --agent, replicate uses $SYMBOLON_AGENT, then Claude Code in headless mode. --prompt FILE replaces the default prompt; $pack, $build and $components in it are filled in.

The agent is not sandboxed. It runs with your permissions, and the work directory only keeps it from seeing the original code if it stays there. For a clean room, run replicate on a machine or container that has no copy of the original.

items.title: What comes out
items.text:
replication-1/
  replication.json          the report
  builds/<build>/           each agent's work directory: pack/, build/, agent.log
  attestations/<component>.<build>.json
  diff/<component>.json     the full diff report
  holdout/<build>/          the holdout copies that ran

✓ build claude-1  claude, 412s, 8/8 components built
✓ build other-2  other, 388s, 8/8 components built
✓ search-query  2/2 builds passed, holdout 2/2  ambiguity 0.0000, vs reference claude-1 0.0000, other-2 0.0000, 0 split(s)
✗ bibtex-import  2/2 builds passed, holdout 2/2
    ambiguity 0.0153, 1 split(s)
    1. claude-1 | other-2  31 inputs; no obligation covers it, a gap in the pack
...
not converged: 1 split(s) to review

Each split is labelled:

Label Meaning What to do gap The disagreeing inputs trace to no obligation Decide the point: add a decided or default obligation with a check, or mark it open weak-check They trace to a decided or default obligation, whose checks both builds pass Add the witness as an example, or tighten the property review They trace only to other obligations Look at the witness

A split on a point the pack marks open is allowed, but diff cannot trace an input to an open obligation, since open obligations have no checks. The builders' readings.toml entries name the obligation they chose a reading for; the report's readings section shows where they chose differently.

The run converges when every build passes every component and its holdout, and the builds agree on every input diff tried. Convergence shows the pack is clear, not that it is right: builders can share a wrong default. The reference, the holdout and counterexamples cover that.

The command exits 1 when a build fails a component or its holdout, or when --max-ambiguity is given and a component's ambiguity is above it.

items.title: Writing a contract
items.text: This walks through a contract from symbolon init to a valid digest. The full rules are in the contract format.

items.title: 1. Scaffold
items.text:
symbolon init acme/shout --author "you@example.com"

This creates contracts/acme/shout/versions/1/ with every required file and a reference implementation, and it already passes validate. Change one file at a time and re-run symbolon validate contracts/acme/shout/versions/1 after each.

items.title: 2. Describe the capability
items.text:
Edit symbolon.toml. The description is the prose half of the spec: write what a builder needs to know that the schema cannot say, such as which inputs are invalid and what happens at the edges. Declare anything the implementation needs from the world under [requires]. Empty lists mean no network, no credentials and no state.

Unknown keys are errors, so a typo cannot silently change a contract's meaning.

items.title: 3. Define the interface
items.text:
schema.py defines pydantic Input and Output models. Use ConfigDict(extra="forbid") and Field(description=...) so the generated JSON Schema is strict and self-explaining. Then regenerate the language-neutral schema:

symbolon schema contracts/acme/shout/versions/1

validate fails if schema/*.json drifts from schema.py.

items.title: 4. Add examples
items.text:
examples.jsonl holds one case per line:

{"input": {"text": "hi"}, "output": {"text": "HI"}}
{"input": {"text": ""}, "raises": "ValueError", "note": "empty input is invalid"}

Examples pin exact behaviour at specific points, including the awkward ones. There must be at least two with different outputs.

items.title: 5. Write properties
items.text:
Each test_* function in properties.py takes impl as its first parameter and usually uses hypothesis @given:

from hypothesis import given, strategies as st
from schema import Input

@given(text=st.text(min_size=1))
def test_output_is_upper_case(impl, text):
    assert impl(Input(text=text)).text == text.upper()

Don't use @settings: the seed and the example budget come from [spec] in the manifest, so runs are reproducible.

The vacuity check is the one most often hit. If your properties only check the output's type, an implementation that returns a constant passes them, and validate rejects the contract:

@given(text=st.text())
def test_returns_text(impl, text):
    assert isinstance(impl(Input(text=text)).text, str)   # vacuous

When every check passes, validate prints the alias and the digest. That digest is what implementations pin and attestations name.
